description: Solo explorer - not in search for other team members
summary:
even Sols is a ten-minute browser game for students. The player controls the energy of a small Mars station for one week (seven sols). Solar panels charge a battery in the day. With three sliders the player sends this energy to oxygen, heat and the radiation shield. Cold nights, a dust storm and solar flares arrive, and the player must keep the crew safe.

The game answers the challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer”. Students balance power, life support and shielding, and they see how one choice changes the others.

This is important because astronauts on Mars will live with limited energy. Our game lets students feel this problem and learn to plan ahead.
details:
Project description

Seven Sols is a game in one web page. It works in a browser on a phone or a computer. There is nothing to install.

The player manages the energy of a small station on Mars for seven sols. A sol is one day on Mars. The week is real: 7–13 September 2017. On 10 September a very strong solar flare (class X8.2) happened on the Sun, and its particles reached Mars. In the game the week takes ten minutes. The player can pause the game or make it 2 or 4 times faster.

The screen shows the station, four bars and three sliders. The bars are the battery, oxygen, heat and the radiation shield. Each slider sends energy to one system: make oxygen, heat the station or charge the shield. The goal is to keep oxygen, heat and the shield above the red minimum line until the end of sol 7.

How it works

Energy. Solar panels work from 06:00 to 18:00 and give the most power at noon. Dust in the air takes away a part of this power. The battery holds up to 90 kWh. At night the station lives only on the battery. A night uses almost a full battery if the player only keeps the bars at the same level. So a good player stores oxygen, heat and shield charge in the day, when the Sun gives more energy than the station needs.

Three systems. The crew uses oxygen all the time at the same speed. The station loses heat faster when it is colder outside. The shield loses charge faster when the radiation is higher: the walls of the station stop a part of the radiation, and the shield must stop the rest. In the solar storm the radiation is about two times higher, and the shield has up to six times more work. A slider at a higher level fills its bar faster and uses more energy. At full power oxygen takes 5 kW, heat takes 10 kW and the shield takes 12 kW.

Data table. The game has a small table from Mars with one row for each day: the coldest air temperature of the sol, the dust level (tau) and the radiation level. It also has two times from the table: when the radiation started to grow and when it dropped. From these points the game draws a line for every hour. The temperature is the coldest at sunrise and the warmest in the afternoon. The radiation is flat before the storm, grows to the peak and then goes down. The dust level is the same for the whole sol. The points are real numbers. The lines between them are our model.

Planning. A tape at the bottom of the screen shows the forecast for the next hours: the Sun, the temperature outside and the radiation. Dots on the tape mark the numbers from the table. The player can see a cold night or the solar storm before it comes and save energy in time. Small triangles on each slider show the level where the bar stops changing. Short messages warn about danger, for example: “Solar storm in 6 h: charge the shield.”

Crew health. When a bar is below its minimum, the crew loses health. The lower the bar, the faster the loss. Health does not come back. If health falls to zero, the mission stops. The score is the crew health at the end of the week. The end screen shows how many hours a bar was below the minimum, how long the battery was empty and how much energy was lost with a full battery. It also gives one tip for the next try.

What benefits it has

  • Students learn by doing. In ten minutes they feel a real problem of a Mars base: there is not enough energy for everything at the same time.
  • They learn to plan ahead. A good player reads the forecast and gets ready before the night and before the storm.
  • They meet real space weather: the solar storm of September 2017, with numbers measured on Mars.
  • They learn to read graphs: how sunlight, temperature and radiation change in time.
  • It is easy to use in class: one link, any phone or computer, ten minutes. The game also works as one file with no internet.

What we hope to achieve

We want students to understand that life on Mars depends on energy and good planning. Our next steps:

  • add more real weeks from Mars, for example a week with a dust storm;
  • add a station on the Moon;
  • add a mode for two players.

What is real and what is a model

The numbers in the data table are real: they are measurements, or values read from a NASA graph (see “NASA Data”). The lines between the points, the size of the battery, the power of the systems and the rules for crew health and for the shield are our game model. They are not NASA measurements. The game is hard on purpose, but it can be won. Our test bots show it: a player who stores supplies in the day and gets ready for the storm keeps the crew at 100% health.

How we used AI

Nikita Gavrilov made the core of the game himself: the idea, the structure of the game, the main story, the ideas for the look of the game, the first data, and the logic that connects all the numbers of the station. He built the first version of the game in Scratch (the original Scratch project is downloaded to the project folder, link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1z8HobwpFexvZCThuLWStfvBQXuAI-cnu?usp=drive_link).

An AI tool (Claude) helped with two things. It moved Nikita’s game to the web: it wrote the code of the web version from his game. And it drew the pictures from his ideas. AI search also helped to find the numbers in NASA sources. The pictures have a visible mark “Made with AI”, and the game page says this in its text and in its metadata.

Tools

  • Scratch: Nikita built the first version of the game in it.
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web version. No game engine and no libraries. The pictures are SVG drawings made in code.
  • A spreadsheet for the data table and Python (openpyxl) to put its numbers into the game.
  • Node.js test bots that play the whole week with different plans. They helped us make the game hard but fair.
  • Playwright and Google Chrome to test the game on phone and computer screens.
  • The font Sofia Sans Condensed from Google Fonts.
  • Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. We used SI tools: Claude, a large language model (an AI assistant) made by Anthropic.

What we did ourselves. Nikita Gavrilov, made the core of the game himself: the idea, the structure of the game, the main story, the ideas for the look of the game, the first data, and the logic that connects all the numbers. He built the first version of the game in Scratch. A crew lives on a Mars station for one week. Energy comes from solar panels in the day. The player sends it to oxygen, heat and the radiation shield with three sliders. Dust cuts solar power. The cold and the radiation come from a data table. The whole week takes ten minutes. He also decided to play a real week on Mars with a solar storm: 7–13 September 2017.

What AI did with us:

  • Claude moved Nikita’s game to the web: it wrote the code of the web version (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) from his game;
  • Claude drew the pictures of the station and of Mars as SVG code, from Nikita’s ideas;
  • an AI tool helped us to find the numbers in NASA sources and to put them into one table, and we kept the source links;
  • in the web version Claude tuned the numbers for the real week, such as the battery size and the rule of the shield, and tested them with test bots;
  • Claude suggested some details: the crew health score, the forecast tape, the triangles on the sliders and the short messages;
  • Claude built the slides and wrote the first version of the texts on this page, which we then checked.

How we mark it. The pictures made with AI have a visible mark “Made with AI”. The start screen of the game says “An AI tool made the art and the code and helped to collect the data table”, and the same is written in the metadata of the page. We did not use NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
